bib.title: Learning to Compress Prompts with Gist Tokens
bib.venue: NeurIPS 2023 (37th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems)

read.skipped: References skimmed for lineage; Listing A.3 examples 1-10 read but not analysed beyond noting no new results

question: Can an LM be trained to compress a prompt into a few cached gist tokens that generalise to unseen prompts, cutting inference cost with little loss in output quality?
hypothesis: Restricting attention so tokens after the gist tokens cannot see the prompt forces the LM to compress the prompt into the gist activations during ordinary instruction finetuning.
contributions: Gisting: predict a compressed prompt prefix zero-shot, amortising both inference-time prompting cost and per-task distillation cost
A masking-only way to learn gist models with no extra training cost over instruction finetuning
Up to 26x prompt compression, 40% FLOPs reduction and 4.2% wall-time speedup with minimal quality loss on LLaMA-7B and FLAN-T5-XXL

method.summary: Insert k copies of a new gist token between the prompt and the input, and mask attention so input and output tokens cannot attend to prompt tokens. Finetune LLaMA-7B and FLAN-T5-XXL on Alpaca+ with this mask; the gist-token key/value activations then serve as a cacheable compressed prompt. Quality is compared with positive/negative controls and a TF-IDF keyword baseline using ROUGE-L, ChatGPT-3.5 and human pairwise judgments.
method.task: instruction following with prompt compression (instruction finetuning with gist masking)

datasets.name: Alpaca+ (Self-Instruct + Stanford Alpaca)
datasets.size: 130,321 examples; 104,664 unique tasks; 48,530 unique inputs; 0-5 inputs per task (0.64 avg); ~59% of tasks have no input
datasets.preprocessing: examples over max length truncated from the end (<1% truncated); empty inputs omitted

datasets.name: Alpaca+ Human validation
datasets.size: 252 prompts (83% non-empty inputs); human eval on random 100
datasets.split: hand-written Self-Instruct prompts and gold completions
datasets.preprocessing: avg train prompt ~20 tokens vs ~26 in this split

models.name: LLaMA-7B gist
models.vocab: base vocab plus one gist token
models.context: max sequence length 512 during training/eval (768 on Human split)

models.name: FLAN-T5-XXL gist
models.vocab: base vocab plus one gist token
models.context: max input 128, max output 256 (384/384 on Human split)

models.name: Positive control
models.architecture: same, 1 gist token, no mask change (standard instruction finetuning)

models.name: Negative control
models.architecture: trained without access to the task t

models.name: TF-IDF
models.architecture: instruction replaced by first subword token of its top TF-IDF keyword; standard finetuning

training.objective: standard instruction-finetuning LM loss (autoregressive on y) with gist attention mask; viewed as meta context distillation, L_G = E_{t,x}[KL(p_LM(y|t,x) || p_G(y|G(t),x))]
training.hardware: 4x A100-SXM4-80GB, 480GB RAM, 16 CPUs; DeepSpeed ZeRO stage 3

other.deepspeed: subgroup size 1e9, max live params 1e9, max reuse distance 1e9
other.hyperparameter_source: LLaMA identical to Alpaca; FLAN-T5 identical to Tk-Instruct except lr 5e-5 instead of 1e-5
other.note: no substantial gains training beyond 1 epoch for FLAN-T5-XXL

inference.decoding: greedy; beam search B=4 gave limited gains
inference.samples: inferred: one greedy output per item, single run; seeds not stated
inference.prompting: input is (task t, gist tokens g1..gk, input x)

parameters.compression_factor: avg token length of validation split / number of gist tokens

other.efficiency_benchmark: single forward pass (one decode step with one input token), PyTorch 2.0, 1 A100, averaged over 252 Human instructions; caching strategies None / Instruction / Gist

metrics.name: ROUGE-L
metrics.definition: lexical overlap with reference; text-davinci completions as reference, gold human reference on Human split

metrics.name: ChatGPT win rate
metrics.definition: ChatGPT-3.5 picks the better of gist model vs positive control (random A/B order, ties allowed); 50% = parity

metrics.name: Human win rate
metrics.definition: same pairwise judgement by 3 Prolific annotators on 100 Human-split examples, IDK dropped

metrics.name: Cohen's kappa
metrics.definition: linearly weighted agreement among annotators and ChatGPT

metrics.name: CUDA time / GFLOPs
metrics.definition: per forward pass profiling with different caching strategies

eval.protocol: Fig 3 error bars are 95% exact binomial CIs, ties split equally and rounded down in favour of positive control; human eval via Prolific, IRB approved; single training run per configuration apparently (no seeds reported)

availability.data: Alpaca+ outputs and ChatGPT judgments at same repo

prompts.purpose: ChatGPT pairwise judge system prompt, opening (4 worked examples and JSON-format instruction follow; see Listing A.2)
prompts.text: Given a user instruction and two AI assistant responses, your job is to select the response that is more helpful, and give reasons why. Judge responses holistically, paying special attention to whether the response (1) correctly follows the provided instruction and (2) is factually accurate. If both responses are equal, you may call a tie, but please use this response sparingly.

results.claim: Gist models compress prompts up to 26x with output quality near the uncompressed positive control (abstract claim).
results.setup: LLaMA-7B and FLAN-T5-XXL, single gist token, Human split (avg prompt ~26 tokens)
results.quote: gisting enables up to 26x compression of prompts, resulting in up to 40% FLOPs reductions, 4.2% wall time speedups, and storage savings, all with minimal loss in output quality

results.claim: LLaMA-7B single-gist ChatGPT win rate vs positive control on Seen prompts.
results.metric: ChatGPT win rate vs positive control
results.setup: LLaMA-7B, 1 gist token, Seen split (1000 prompts, unseen inputs); 50% = parity with positive control
results.quote: 48.6% and 50.8% win rates for LLaMA-7B and FLAN-T5-XXL
results.note: FLAN-T5-XXL is 50.8 on the same split

results.claim: Unseen-prompt win rates against positive control stay close to parity.
results.metric: ChatGPT win rate vs positive control
results.setup: Unseen split (1000 prompts within Alpaca+ distribution), 1 gist token
results.quote: 49.7% (LLaMA) and 46.2% (FLAN-T5) win rates against the positive controls

results.claim: On the OOD Human split win rates drop slightly.
results.metric: ChatGPT win rate vs positive control
results.setup: Human split (252 hand-written Self-Instruct prompts), 1 gist token
results.quote: slight drops in win rate to 45.8% (LLaMA) and 42.5% (FLAN-T5)

results.claim: ROUGE-L, LLaMA-7B Human split: Pos 27.0, Gist 23.9, TF-IDF 16.5, Neg 14.4 (gist 75.4 normalised).
results.setup: LLaMA-7B, single gist token, Human split, references = gold human completions
results.table: Table 1, row LLaMA-7B Gist, column Human ROUGE-L

results.claim: ROUGE-L, LLaMA-7B Unseen split: Gist 46.6 vs Pos 48.1; Seen: Gist 57.8 vs Pos 58.0.
results.setup: LLaMA-7B, single gist token, Unseen split
results.table: Table 1, row LLaMA-7B Gist, column Unseen ROUGE-L

results.claim: ROUGE-L, FLAN-T5-XXL: Gist 48.9 (Seen), 43.8 (Unseen), 21.7 (Human) vs Pos 50.6, 45.7, 23.9.
results.setup: FLAN-T5-XXL, single gist token, Human split
results.table: Table 1, row FLAN-T5-XXL Gist, column Human ROUGE-L

results.claim: TF-IDF discrete compression is only marginally better than the negative control.
results.metric: ChatGPT win rate vs positive control
results.setup: LLaMA-7B Human split; TF-IDF = first subword of one keyword, same compression as 1 gist token; Neg = 22.2; Gist = 45.8
results.quote: gist compression is vastly superior to discrete compression; the TF-IDF models in Table 1 only marginally outperform the negative control models across the board.

results.claim: Number of gist tokens barely matters; 10 tokens can hurt.
results.setup: k in {1,2,5,10}, both models, Figure 3
results.quote: Models were generally insensitive to the number of gist tokens k: compressing prompts into a single token prefix did not substantially underperform larger prefixes.

results.claim: Gist caching cuts FLOPs by 40% versus no caching, for both models.
results.setup: One forward pass (one decode step, one input token), PyTorch 2.0, 1x A100 80GB, averaged over 252 Human instructions; LLaMA 915 -> 552 GFLOPs, FLAN-T5 716 -> 427
results.quote: Gist caching improves significantly over unoptimized models, with 40% FLOPs savings and 4-7% lower wall time for both models.

results.claim: CUDA wall-time saving versus no caching: 6.8% LLaMA-7B, 4.2% FLAN-T5-XXL.
results.metric: CUDA time reduction vs no caching
results.setup: As above; Gist 21.8 ms (LLaMA), 29.7 ms (FLAN)
results.table: Table 3, rows CUDA time (ms), column Gist vs. None

results.claim: Versus caching the uncompressed instruction in the KV cache (LLaMA only), gisting gives negligible FLOPs saving and about 1% wall time.
results.setup: LLaMA-7B, avg KV cache 26 (instruction) vs 1 (gist); wall time 22.1 -> 21.8 ms (1.0%)
results.quote: a negligible decrease in FLOPs (0.11%) and a modest 1% speedup in wall time.

results.claim: Predicted FLOPs gain from Chinchilla-style equations matches the observed one.
results.metric: predicted relative FLOPs improvement of gist caching
results.setup: LLaMA-7B, KV cache compression rate 26, modified Chinchilla FLOPs equations
results.quote: the Chinchilla equations predict a relative improvement of Gist caching of 0.12%.

results.claim: KV cache cost per token for LLaMA-7B, so gisting allows caching up to 26x more prompts in the same storage.
results.setup: fp32: 4 bytes x 2 (K+V) x 32 layers x 32 heads x 128 head dim
results.quote: for LLaMA-7B, each token in the KV cache requires 1.05 MB storage.

results.claim: Human annotators agree with ChatGPT judge on average win rate.
results.metric: Gist win rate over positive control, human average
results.setup: 100 of 252 Human-split examples, 3 Prolific annotators each, ~10% 'I Don't Know' dropped
results.quote: human annotators agree with ChatGPT, with average win rates of 52.3% (vs. 48.0%) for LLaMA-7B and 40.6% (vs. 42.0%) for FLAN-T5-XXL.

results.claim: Inter-annotator agreement is low but ChatGPT agrees with humans about as well as humans agree with each other.
results.setup: Linearly weighted Cohen's kappa, Human split subset
results.quote: The average pairwise Cohen’s κ among human annotators is .24 for LLaMA-7B and .33 for FLAN-T5-XXL.

results.claim: Gist outputs match the positive control exactly only on seen tasks.
results.metric: exact string match with positive control
results.setup: Single-token gist models, Fig A.3
results.quote: the gist model outputs exactly match the positive control nearly 50% of the time. This drops to ~20–25% for Unseen tasks and ~10% for the OOD Human tasks.

results.claim: Failure modes: loss of specific detail and runaway generations.
results.setup: Human split, qualitative examples (FLAN-T5 outputs 'Culture' vs 'Arts & Culture'; LLaMA repeats \subparagraph for hundreds of tokens)
results.quote: We also see more cases of runaway generations that do not occur with the positive control model:

results.claim: Gist masking is a small code change at no extra training cost.
results.setup: Decoder-only and encoder-decoder LMs
results.quote: Overall, these masking changes are extremely simple and can be implemented in roughly 10 source lines of code.

results.claim: Encoder-decoder generalises slightly worse OOD; authors' explanation is untested.
results.setup: FLAN-T5 vs LLaMA, Human split
results.quote: Future work will be needed to investigate this hypothesis.

results.claim: Cost of the judging: ChatGPT judgments and human study.
results.setup: ~22.5k ChatGPT judgments; 3 annotators x 100 examples at $14.35/hour
results.quote: In total, we collected ~22.5k judgments from ChatGPT for an estimated cost of $29.28.

limits: Authors concede gisting loses nuance of the original instruction (Sec 5.1 failure case) and practitioners should evaluate the compute/accuracy tradeoff before deployment.
Prompts are short (~20-26 tokens); no long prompts, few-shot prompts, documents or conversation history tested, though authors say biggest gains would come from long prompts (future work).
Requires finetuning the LM itself; retrofitting a frozen LM with a separate compressor is future work.
Only LLaMA-7B and FLAN-T5-XXL; training data is synthetic GPT-3 Alpaca+ (~59% of tasks have no input).
Quality judged by ChatGPT-3.5, ROUGE-L and 100 examples with 3 humans (low kappa .24-.33); no downstream benchmarks.
Wall-time benchmarks are single-step decoding at small scale; larger batch/sequence gains are expected but not measured.
Gain over plain instruction KV caching is small for LLaMA (0.11% FLOPs, 1% time); main benefit is storage and context space.
Dated: LLaMA-1 and ChatGPT-3.5 (Mar-Apr 2023); context windows have since grown (reader inference, not the paper's).

figures.caption: Prompting retains the multitask capabilities of LMs, but is inefficient. Finetuning/distillation is more efficient, but requires training a model for each task. Gisting compresses prompts into activations on top of gist tokens, saving compute and generalizing to novel tasks at test time.
figures.why: contrasts prompting, finetuning and gisting at a glance

figures.caption: Gist Masking. Attention mask modifications for (a) decoder-only and (b) encoder-decoder Transformer LMs to encourage prompt compression into gist tokens.
figures.why: the whole method is the mask pattern

figures.caption: Varying the number of gist tokens. ROUGE-L and ChatGPT scores for (a) LLaMA-7B and (b) FLAN-T5-XXL for different gist tokens.
figures.why: shows k barely matters and compression factors 2x-26x

figures.caption: FLOPs for each operation in a single layer of self attention with a 2000-length KV cache (LLaMA-7B).
figures.why: explains why gist caching saves little FLOPs over instruction caching

post_gist_mask = make_mask_pre_first_gist(inputs, gist_token, dtype=torch.bool)[:, None, None]

mask = torch.where(pre_gist_time_mask, pre_gist_mask, post_gist_mask)
